previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: An elderly female with a history of chronic left-sided chest pain, diastolic heart failure, recurrent pulmonary embolism on anticoagulation, and prior gastrointestinal bleeding presented with an exacerbation of her typical burning chest pain, which worsened with deep breathing and was associated with left arm and jaw discomfort. Initial evaluation ruled out acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, and aortic pathology via normal EKG, serial cardiac enzymes, and a negative CTA. The pain was determined to be musculoskeletal, consistent with costochondritis, and not cardiac in origin. She was found to have acute on chronic iron deficiency anemia with trace guaiac-positive stools, likely due to chronic gastritis exacerbated by intermittent NSAID use and long-term anticoagulation. Despite the bleeding risk, warfarin was continued due to high thrombotic risk, while omeprazole was uptitrated to 40 mg twice daily and iron supplementation was initiated. NSAIDs were discontinued, and she was referred to gastroenterology for outpatient endoscopic evaluation. Her heart failure and hypertension remained stable, managed on home medications. She was discharged home with improved pain control and stable hemoglobin, on a revised medication regimen emphasizing GI protection and safe analgesia with acetaminophen.

undergo repeat endoscopy except if she were to develop a life 
threatening bleed. H pylori was sent and returned positive, 
however, in further discussion with her HCP, she was treated for 
H pylori infection last year so treatment was not repeated.  
Her INR was reversed.  She was transfused a total of 4 units 
PRBCs, slowly given cardiac status, with steady increase in her 
Hct from 18.4 on admission to 28.5.  Her energy level and mental 
status improved dramatically with transfusion.  She was treated 
with IV lasix twice for shortness of breath/volume overload.   
She was continued on her PPI.  Outpatient GI follow was arranged 
to discuss further options to prevent recurrence and 
consideration of further evaluation/treatment of H pylori.  

2. Coagulopathy / Recurrent DVT/PE: INR 6 on admission. She is 
on coumadin for history of provoked DVT in the past and 
unprovoked PE. INR was reversed with vitamin K and 2 units of 
FFP.  Her HCP notes that her appetitie had been poor recently; 
decreased vitamin K intake is the likely etiology of her INR 
elevation.  I had a long discussion with her HCP about risks and 
benefits of treatment options - eg, continueing coumadin with 
close monitoring of INR vs discontinuing coumadin and placing 
IVC filter.  He prefers for the patient to not have invasive 
procedures if possible and would like to continue coumadin.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted with severe anemia.  This was likely due to 
recurrnet bleeding from your GI tract in the setting of an 
elevated INR (coumadin level) of 6.  You refused to have a 
repeat endoscopy or colonoscopy.  You were transfused 4 units of 
blood with improvement in your fatigue and your blood counts. 
You had no further bleeding.  
Your coumadin was held.  We discussed several options to try to 
prevent this from happening again and you prefer to restart your 
coumadin now; please discuss this with your PCP at your follow 
up visit to determine if this is a medication you should 
continue taking, or if perhaps it might be reasonable to 
discontinue this medication in the future given your recurrent 
episodes of bleeding (in that case you might be a candidate for 
an ""IVC filter"" as we discussed). 
We have not changed your medicines.  Please have your INR 
checked on ___.  Your coumadin level (INR) is likely to go 
up again if you are not eating well.  If you notice that you are 
not eating very well, please call the HCA anticoagulation nurses 
to arrange an extra INR check and perhaps to lower your coumadin 
dose.  This is very important because if your INR is elevated 
again you might have recurrent life threatening bleeding. 
Weigh yourself every morning, call MD if weight goes up more 
than 3 lbs.
